content:
I'm a big fan of the moment when, years into a gaming subgenre's existence, people start rethinking what those games are capable of. All the expected ideas, they've been done, so the latecomers are by necessity inventors if they want to stand out. All Will Rise is one of them. In essence, it's a deck-building card game that was volcanoed into existence by the popularity of Slay the Spire several years ago, or perhaps Magic: The Gathering before, or perhaps Pokémon. Although to compare it to any of those would be misleading, because it's got more in common with courtroom drama series Phoenix Wright.
Made by Speculative Agency, and touting star-quality talent like award-winning writer and narrative designer Meghna Jayanth (80 Days, Sable, Thirsty Suitors), All Will Rise follows hot-shot and sometimes hot-headed lawyer Kuyili in her battle against greedy corporations, which are inadvertently - or perhaps deliberately - destroying the natural world around them. In this case they've literally and quite spectacularly set a river on fire. There's out-of-court action as you build a case against someone - read: build your deck of cards to use against them - then there's courtroom action as you deploy your card-claims and make your winning arguments.
It really is very Phoenix Wright, both in its presentation and in terms of the energy it exudes. It's not anime - it has a different kind of sketched but vividly colourful style - but the way character cut-outs appear with text boxes next to them is very reminiscent. There are no stuffy silences and dusty courtrooms and ridiculous wigs. The game is lively and modern, with Kuyili delivering arguments like punches and her opponents returning in kind. Words appear with a spoken rhythm, injecting life into them, and visibly rattle and shake as if with emotion. Words: All Will Rise knows how to use them.
But how do you use the cards? This one's trickier because, well, court cases are tricky. There's a lot to them, and so there are lots of cards here. As far as I understand based on the demo, cards are claims (or rhetoric or denials) you make while arguing, and have evolving strengths - 'disproven' through to 'undeniable' - based on other cards played around them, and if you've strengthened your arguments outside of court. The more evolved a card, the stronger it is, and the more it affects three core attributes when played: hearts, minds, guts. When these are pushed to their limits, they trigger a dramatic argument to be made, potentially winning the case or at least significantly moving it forwards.
I don't understand all of the synergies and complexities yet, but All Will Rise helps you a lot early on, suggesting what to play and serve. There are buff cards and manoeuvres being played that I can see are working but I don't know why, but then I wouldn't expect to understand all of the intricacies of a card game this early on. It's a good sign; it suggests depth. But a key thing to understand about the card 'battles' is you're not always trying to defeat someone.
![A court room with Indian styling. Large, ornate, airy, but intricate and carved and bathed in warm sunshine. A screenshot from All Will Rise](https://assetsio.gnwcdn.com/all-will-rise_WH6lp7O.jpg?width=2048&height=2048&fit=bounds&quality=85&format=jpg&auto=webp)
For instance, a major outside-court mission in the demo involves going to see a kind of mystic woman who claims to speak - or be in touch with - a river god. As in, the river that's on fire. I'm going to see if I can get some testimony or information to help my case, because maybe she's seen something. But before she'll give me anything, I need to convince her she should, which requires a whole courtroom-like debate where she puts forward arguments and I counter them, as I try to, well, outplay her. But I'm not trying to defeat her: I'm trying to get her on side. And I like this approach: it broadens what the game can do.
As much of the game happens outside the courtroom as in it, then, it seems. Outside is where you discuss cases and chat with your legal team besties, Shintu and Joy, who you banter with and who send you on independent missions to gather evidence. It's also where you learn about the world around you, which is a big part of the game's allure. All Will Rise is set in a fictitious place, a make-believe world called Muziris, but it could so easily be Mumbai or a port city in India. The presentation, the unabashed colouring, the rich warmth, the culture and themes - they all scream Indian, and lend All Will Rise a sense of immediate difference. Though the issues the game tackles are universal.
You see, All Will Rise is a game for change. Indeed, Speculative Agency is a studio focused on making games for change. All Will Rise's perspective is that mega corporations should answer for the consequences of their destructive actions, which is one of the reasons Speculative Agency handed back the funding it once received from Xbox to make the game, because of Microsoft's links to Israel and, thus, the genocide in Gaza. "Our game is also about ecocide and corporate greed," the studio said at the time. "How do we strike the balance between our themes, integrity, consistency and, frankly, our interest in making a commercial indie game?"
That does not mean that All Will Rise is preachy, nor that it is first and foremost focused on this agenda. Yes, an anti-greed and therefore anti-capitalist message underpins its story, but its success comes in appealing as a game first - through lively dialogue and engrossing card play, and in the depth of its themes underneath. That there's a purposeful message doesn't interfere with that. Indeed, as far as I'm concerned, it strengthens it. It's nice to see a game unafraid to have a perspective.
